qaPairs.question: How do you evaluate a RAG system? What metrics do you use?
qaPairs.answer:
RAG evaluation has two parts — retrieval quality and generation quality. Retrieval metrics: (1) Hit Rate / Recall@K — does the correct chunk appear in the top K results? (2) MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) — how high is the correct chunk ranked? (3) NDCG — measures ranking quality considering relevance grades. Generation metrics: (4) Faithfulness — does the answer stick to the retrieved context? No hallucination? (5) Answer Relevancy — does the answer actually address the question? (6) Context Relevancy — are the retrieved chunks relevant to the question? (7) Context Utilization — does the answer use all relevant retrieved information? The RAGAS framework automates all of these using LLM-as-judge.
Example:
Evaluating a customer support RAG:
Test set: 200 questions with ground truth answers
Retrieval evaluation:
Hit Rate@5: 0.87 (87% of time, correct chunk in top 5) MRR: 0.72 (correct chunk is usually ranked 1st or 2nd)
Generation evaluation (using RAGAS):
Faithfulness: 0.91 (91% of claims are grounded in context) Answer Relevancy: 0.88 (88% of answers address the question) Context Relevancy: 0.79 (21% of retrieved context is irrelevant)
Diagnosis:
Retrieval is good (87% hit rate) But context has noise (79% relevancy) -> need better reranking Faithfulness is strong -> LLM is grounding well Action: Add Cohere reranker to improve context relevancy to 90%+
Interview Tip: Mention RAGAS by name. Say 'I use RAGAS with Faithfulness, Answer Relevancy, and Context Relevancy as my core evaluation metrics.' This is the industry standard framework — mentioning it shows production experience.

qaPairs.question: What is RAGAS and how does it work?
qaPairs.answer:
RAGAS (Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment) is an open-source framework that evaluates RAG pipelines using LLM-based metrics. It doesn't need human-labeled ground truth for most metrics — it uses the LLM itself to assess quality. Core metrics: (1) Faithfulness — breaks the answer into claims, checks if each claim is supported by the context. Score 0-1. (2) Answer Relevancy — generates questions from the answer, checks if they match the original question. If yes, the answer is relevant. (3) Context Precision — are the retrieved chunks relevant? Checks ranking quality. (4) Context Recall — does the retrieved context contain all info needed to answer? Compares against ground truth. You can run RAGAS on hundreds of test queries automatically to get a system-wide quality score.
Example:
Using RAGAS in Python:
from ragas import evaluate from ragas.metrics import faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision results = evaluate( dataset=test_dataset, # questions + retrieved contexts + answers metrics=[faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision] )
Output:
faithfulness: 0.89 answer_relevancy: 0.92 context_precision: 0.78
Interpretation:
Answers are mostly grounded (0.89 faithfulness) -> good
Answers address the question well (0.92) -> good
But retrieval precision is low (0.78) -> too much irrelevant context
Action: improve chunking or add reranking to boost context_precision
Interview Tip: Say 'I run RAGAS evaluation before and after every RAG pipeline change to measure impact.' This shows you have a systematic approach to improvement, not just guesswork.

qaPairs.question: How do you create a test set for RAG evaluation?
qaPairs.answer:
Three approaches: (1) Manual creation — domain experts write 50-200 question-answer pairs from the knowledge base. Gold standard but slow and expensive. (2) Synthetic generation — use an LLM to read your documents and generate question-answer pairs automatically. Fast and scalable. Tools: RAGAS test set generation, LlamaIndex. Generates diverse questions (simple factual, multi-hop reasoning, complex). (3) Production logs — collect real user queries + thumbs up/down feedback. Most realistic but requires existing traffic. Best practice: start with synthetic (fast baseline), supplement with 50-100 manual expert pairs, then continuously add from production logs. Always include: edge cases (questions with no answer in docs), multi-hop questions (requiring info from multiple chunks), and temporal questions (latest vs outdated info).
Example:
Creating a test set for a legal RAG system:
Synthetic generation (100 questions):
Feed contract documents to GPT-4 Prompt: 'Generate 20 questions a lawyer would ask about this contract' -> 'What is the termination clause?' (simple factual) -> 'How do liability limits compare between sections 3 and 7?' (multi-hop) -> 'Is there a non-compete provision?' (yes/no)
Manual expert pairs (50 questions):
Legal team writes tricky questions they know users ask -> 'Does the force majeure clause cover pandemics?' -> 'What happens if payment is 30 days late?' (edge case)
Unanswerable questions (20 questions):
-> 'What is the client's credit score?' (not in the document) Expected answer: 'This information is not available in the contract.' Total: 170 test questions covering diverse scenarios.
Interview Tip: Mention unanswerable questions as part of your test set. 'I always include questions that have no answer in the documents to test if the system says I don't know instead of hallucinating.' This shows production maturity. Production RAG

qaPairs.question: What are the common failure modes of RAG systems in production?
qaPairs.answer:
Seven major failure modes: (1) Wrong chunks retrieved — embedding quality or chunking strategy is off. Fix: better embeddings, reranking, hybrid search. (2) Right chunks but wrong answer — LLM ignores or misinterprets the context. Fix: better prompts, stronger model, structured output. (3) Outdated information — knowledge base not updated. Fix: automated ingestion pipelines, version tracking. (4) Missing information — document wasn't ingested or chunked improperly. Fix: coverage audits, gap analysis. (5) Context overflow — too many chunks stuffed into prompt. Fix: reranking, compression, fewer chunks. (6) Hallucination despite context — LLM adds info not in the chunks. Fix: faithfulness guardrails, citation enforcement. (7) Latency spikes — slow retrieval or generation. Fix: caching, smaller models, pre-computed embeddings.
Example:
Debugging a production RAG failure:
User: 'What is our parental leave policy?' RAG answer: 'Employees get 12 weeks of paid parental leave.' (WRONG: it's 16 weeks)
Debugging steps:
1. Check retrieved chunks -> Found 2020 policy (12 weeks) instead of 2025 (16
weeks)
2. Root cause: Old policy document wasn't deleted after update
3. Both versions exist in vector DB with similar embeddings
4. Old version ranked higher (shorter, more focused text)
Fix:
Delete old policy document from vector DB
Add metadata filter: version='latest'
Add automated pipeline to re-index when docs are updated
Add a freshness score to reranking
Interview Tip: When asked about RAG challenges, don't give a generic answer. Walk through a specific debugging scenario like this. It proves you've actually fixed RAG issues in production.

qaPairs.question: How do you handle document updates and keep the RAG knowledge base fresh?
qaPairs.answer:
Document freshness is a critical production concern. Strategies: (1) Change detection pipeline — monitor source documents for changes (file hash, last modified date). When a doc changes, re-chunk and re-embed only that document. (2) Versioned embeddings — store a version/timestamp with each chunk. When querying, filter for latest version. Keep old versions for audit trail. (3) Incremental ingestion — don't re-embed everything. Only process new/modified/deleted documents. Use document IDs to track what's already indexed. (4) Scheduled refresh — run nightly/weekly batch jobs to sync knowledge base with source systems. (5) TTL (Time to Live) — set expiry on chunks. Auto-delete embeddings older than X days for rapidly changing content. (6) Source of truth validation — periodically verify random samples against source documents.
Example:
Production document update pipeline:
Trigger: Google Drive webhook detects file change -> Step 1: Download updated document -> Step 2: Hash comparison (is content actually different?) -> Step 3: Delete old chunks for this document ID from vector DB -> Step 4: Re-chunk the updated document -> Step 5: Re-embed new chunks -> Step 6: Upsert into vector DB with new version number -> Step 7: Log the update (audit trail) -> Step 8: Run RAGAS eval on 20 sample queries to verify quality Total time: ~2 minutes per document update Result: RAG always has the latest information within minutes of source change.
Interview Tip: Mention 'incremental ingestion' and 'change detection.' Saying 'I don't re-embed everything — I only process changed documents' shows you think about efficiency at scale.

qaPairs.question: How do you add citations and source attribution to RAG answers?
qaPairs.answer:
Citations are critical for trust and verifiability. Methods: (1) Chunk-level citation — tag each retrieved chunk with source document name, page number, and section. After LLM generates, map claims back to source chunks. (2) Inline citation prompting — instruct the LLM: 'After each claim, cite the source as [Source: document_name, page X].' (3) Post-processing citation — after generation, use a separate LLM call to verify which sources support which claims and add citations. (4) Numbered reference — assign numbers to retrieved chunks [1], [2], [3] and instruct LLM to reference them. Most reliable approach: combine inline prompting + post-processing verification. Always include a 'Sources' section at the end of the response.
Example:
System prompt:
'Answer the question using ONLY the provided context. After each claim, cite the source using [Source N]. If the context does not contain the answer, say "I don't have this information."
Context:
[Source 1] HR Policy v2026: "Employees receive 16 weeks paid parental leave." [Source 2] Benefits Guide: "Parental leave can be split into two blocks within 12 months." [Source 3] FAQ: "Both parents are eligible for parental leave."
Generated answer:
'Employees receive 16 weeks of paid parental leave [Source 1]. This leave can be split into two blocks within 12 months of the child\'s birth [Source 2]. Both parents are eligible for this benefit [Source 3].'
Sources:
[1] HR Policy v2026, Section 4.2 [2] Benefits Guide 2026, Page 12 [3] Employee FAQ, Last updated Jan 2026
Interview Tip: Say 'I always enforce citations in RAG systems because users need to verify answers, especially in enterprise, legal, and healthcare domains.' This shows you think about user trust, not just accuracy. Multimodal & Agentic RAG
